question: Is there a conflict about where Aloysius Garcia was at about one o'clock on the night he died?
expected_description: Scott Eccles swears Garcia spoke to him in his bedroom at Wisteria Lodge at nearly one o'clock, but the police say Garcia lay dead on Oxshott Common, nearly a mile away, since one o'clock and before the rain. Garcia cannot be in both places at that time.

involved_claims.what: Garcia looked in at his bedroom door, saying it was nearly one
involved_claims.quote: He apologised for having disturbed me so late, saying that it was nearly one o’clock.

involved_claims.what: he would swear it was Garcia's voice at that hour
involved_claims.quote: I could swear to it that it was he who addressed me in my bedroom at that very hour.

involved_claims.what: Garcia had been dead on the Common since one, before the rain
involved_claims.quote: He had been there since one o’clock. There was rain about that time, and his death had certainly been before the rain.

involved_claims.what: body found on Oxshott Common, about a mile from the house
involved_claims.quote: He was found dead this morning upon Oxshott Common, nearly a mile from his home.

notes: confidence=high. The text itself notes the conflict ('perfectly impossible'); Holmes only hints at an explanation (altered clocks), so the gold finding is the conflict, not its resolution.

question: Where was Lady Brackenstall when Sir Eustace burst into the dining-room: tied to the chair or standing at the window?
expected_description: Lady Brackenstall says she was already bound to the oaken chair at the head of the table when her husband entered. Captain Crocker says she was standing with him just inside the window when Sir Eustace rushed in. She cannot be bound in the chair and standing at the window at the same moment; Holmes concludes she was put in the chair after the death.

involved_claims.what: already tied to the oaken chair at the head of the table
involved_claims.quote: secured me tightly to the oaken chair which stands at the head of the dining-table

involved_claims.what: husband entered after she was bound
involved_claims.quote: It was at this instant that my unfortunate husband entered the room.

involved_claims.what: she stood with him by the window when Sir Eustace came in
involved_claims.quote: I was standing with her just inside the window, in all innocence, as God is my judge, when he rushed like a madman into the room

involved_claims.what: places her in the chair only after the death
involved_claims.quote: No, no, she was placed in the chair _after_ the death of her husband.

notes: confidence=medium. Clean as a place conflict only once Crocker's confession is read; before that Holmes derives it from the blood mark.

question: Is McFarlane's account of spending the night at an hotel compatible with the thumb-mark in Oldacre's hall?
expected_description: McFarlane says he left through the French window and slept at the Anerley Arms; the housekeeper says his hat was left in the hall; Lestrade reads a blood thumb-print in the hall as McFarlane fetching his hat after the crime. On the evidence as presented, McFarlane is both away at the hotel and inside the hall after the crime. Holmes later shows the print was planted, so the conflict is in the evidence as presented, not in the truth.

involved_claims.what: left by the French window, spent the night at the Anerley Arms
involved_claims.quote: so I spent the night at the Anerley Arms

involved_claims.what: his hat and probably stick were left in the hall
involved_claims.quote: Mr. McFarlane had left his hat, and to the best of her belief his stick, in the hall.

involved_claims.what: reads the thumb-mark as McFarlane fetching his hat after the crime
involved_claims.quote: This is where young McFarlane must have come out to get his hat after the crime was done

involved_claims.what: the mark was not there the day before
involved_claims.quote: Only this: that I _know_ that that mark was not there when I examined the hall yesterday.

notes: confidence=low. Borderline R1: the 'two places' are produced by contested evidence, and the text resolves it as a plant. Human decision needed on whether this counts as R1 or as R3.

question: Where was Alec Cunningham when William Kirwan was shot, and does his account fit what Holmes establishes?
expected_description: Alec says he stood at the foot of the stairs inside the house and saw two strangers wrestling outside. Holmes shows the shot was fired from over four yards and that, if Alec's story were right, only Alec himself could have torn the paper from the dead man's hand, i.e. Alec was at the body rather than inside the house watching a stranger.

involved_claims.what: Alec at the foot of the stairs saw two men wrestling outside
involved_claims.quote: as he came to the foot of the stairs he saw two men wrestling together outside

involved_claims.what: if Alec is right, Alec himself must have taken the paper from the dead man
involved_claims.quote: it must have been Alec Cunningham himself, for by the time that the old man had descended several servants were upon the scene

involved_claims.what: fired at over four yards, no powder-blackening
involved_claims.quote: fired from a revolver at the distance of something over four yards

notes: confidence=low. Borderline R1: Holmes argues about sequence and distance, not about a stated alibi. Human decision needed.

question: Are the dates in the Red-Headed League story consistent with each other?
expected_description: Holmes dates the advertisement paper April 27, 1890 and calls it 'just two months ago', which puts the present at late June. But Wilson worked eight weeks and the dissolution notice, found 'this morning', is dated October 9, 1890, and the narrator places the visit in the autumn. The dates cannot all hold.

involved_claims.quote: _The Morning Chronicle_ of April 27, 1890. Just two months ago.

involved_claims.what: the advertisement was shown to him eight weeks before today
involved_claims.quote: Spaulding, he came down into the office just this day eight weeks

involved_claims.what: dissolution notice dated October 9, 1890
involved_claims.quote: THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED. October 9, 1890.

involved_claims.what: the visit took place in the autumn
involved_claims.quote: one day in the autumn of last year

notes: confidence=high that the dates disagree; the arithmetic is mine. Same fact as g029 in questions.jsonl, framed here as a finding task.

question: Do the times given for the Cunningham alarm agree between the police account and Holmes's written statement?
expected_description: The inspector reports the alarm at a quarter to twelve; Holmes's written statement says a quarter to one on Tuesday morning. The text itself calls this a mistake ('It was at a quarter to twelve, as a matter of fact'), so the two times conflict even though the narrative explains it away as a slip.

involved_claims.what: alarm broke out at quarter to twelve
involved_claims.quote: It was quarter to twelve when the alarm broke out.

involved_claims.what: says the attempt was at about a quarter to one
involved_claims.quote: at about a quarter to one on Tuesday morning an attempt was made

involved_claims.what: corrects the mistake: it was a quarter to twelve
involved_claims.quote: It was at a quarter to twelve, as a matter of fact.

notes: confidence=medium. The slip is deliberate on Holmes's part, but a rule layer reading the text cannot know that; the gold answer is that the two times conflict and the text flags it.

'Shortly after' a morning return does not obviously fit a three o'clock departure.
